title: Best Daytona.io alternatives for sandbox environments in 2026
summary: Compare five Daytona alternatives on isolation, idle billing, and persistence, and see what Daytona's 15-minute auto-stop costs.
body_markdown:
Your coding agent finishes a five-minute task. The[Daytona.io](https://www.daytona.io/) sandbox it ran in keeps billing for another quarter of an hour. That's the default auto-stop window. Multiply it across a few thousand sandboxes a day and idle time becomes a line item your finance lead asks about. Or the question comes from security instead. The agent executes code a large language model (LLM) wrote, and someone asks whether that code shares a kernel with[other tenants](https://blaxel.ai/blog/multi-tenant-isolation-ai-agents) .


Both questions land on Daytona because the product changed. The Daytona software started as a self-hosted dev environment manager. Daytona's own account dates the[pivot to AI runtimes](https://www.daytona.io/dotfiles/from-dev-environments-to-ai-runtimes) to December 2024. In June 2026,[core development went private](https://www.daytona.io/dotfiles/updates/daytona-is-going-closed-source) . The Daytona[AI sandbox](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-sandbox) now runs[LLM-generated code](https://blaxel.ai/blog/run-untrusted-llm-generated-code-safely) for agents. That puts it in the same evaluation as E2B, Blaxel, Vercel Sandbox, Cloudflare Sandboxes, and Modal.


For engineering leaders choosing where[production agents execute code](https://blaxel.ai/blog/how-do-ai-agents-execute-code) , this guide covers what Daytona's idle defaults cost and compares five alternatives on isolation and persistence. It closes with how to pick one.


## Key takeaways


- **Active rates are nearly identical:** Daytona, E2B, and Blaxel charge about the same per hour at the same spec, so idle policy decides the bill.
- **Auto-stop is the main cost driver:** Daytona keeps billing idle sandboxes until its auto-stop window ends; tuning it closes most of the gap with Blaxel.
- **Isolation splits into[containers and microVMs](https://blaxel.ai/blog/serverless-vs-containers-vs-micro-vms-ai-agents) :** Daytona defaults to containers. Blaxel, E2B, and Vercel Sandbox run each sandbox in a Firecracker microVM.
- **Persistence limits differ:** Daytona archives stopped containers after a week, and Modal caps lifetime at a day. Cloudflare loses sandbox state after sleep unless you persist it; Blaxel keeps standby state indefinitely.
- **GPUs decide some cases:** Daytona and Modal sell GPU sandboxes; Blaxel is CPU-only.


## Where Daytona fits and where teams outgrow it


Daytona bills per second with[no minimum commitment](https://www.daytona.io/dotfiles/introducing-daytona-cloud-the-agent-native-infrastructure) and gives new accounts free credits. It sells H100 GPU sandboxes alongside container, Linux VM, and Windows classes. Daytona's docs list a[sub-90ms creation figure](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/sandboxes) for the container class using pre-built templates. Its[Trust Center](https://trust.daytona.io/) lists a SOC 2 Type II report. It also lists ISO 27001 and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) coverage. The company closed a[$24 million Series A](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/daytona-raises-24m-series-a-to-give-every-agent-a-computer-302680740.html) in February 2026. For short, bursty, or GPU-heavy jobs, that clears most[procurement checklists](https://blaxel.ai/blog/sandbox-provider-security-assessment-checklist.html) .


The limits start with isolation. The default Daytona sandbox class is a container with[dedicated namespaces](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/isolation) and resource limits. But[agents run code](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-runtime-security) an LLM wrote. For that workload, a microVM runs its own guest kernel. A[container escape](https://blaxel.ai/blog/container-escape) must also breach the microVM boundary to reach the host or a neighboring tenant. Daytona's Linux VM class adds a full kernel, but containers stay the default.[Lifecycle defaults](https://blaxel.ai/blog/sandbox-management-for-ai-coding-agents) are the second limit. Container and GPU sandboxes[auto-stop after 15 minutes](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/persistence) of inactivity. Stopped containers archive after seven days by default, with a 30-day maximum.


You outgrow Daytona when idle time dominates runtime or policy requires[hardware isolation](https://blaxel.ai/blog/tenant-isolation) on every sandbox. The same applies when agents need[state beyond the archive window](https://blaxel.ai/blog/best-platforms-persistent-sandbox-environments) .


## Daytona pricing in 2026: what idle time costs


Item Pricing details


CPU and memory Daytona charges[$0.0504 per vCPU-hour](https://www.daytona.io/pricing) and $0.0162 per GiB-hour of memory.


Example sandbox A sandbox with 1 vCPU and 2 GiB costs about $0.083 per hour while it runs.


Disk Disk adds $0.000108 per GiB-hour after the first 5 GiB free, and stopped or paused sandboxes[bill for disk only](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/billing) .


Credits New accounts get $200 in free credits, and startups can apply for up to $50,000.


GPU An H100 sandbox runs $3.95 per hour, and free credits don't cover GPU sandboxes.


[Idle minutes bill at the same rate as busy ones](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-agent-development-costs) , so the rate card alone won't predict the invoice. Take a pull request (PR) review agent that runs five 5-minute sessions. Seventy-five minutes of waiting sit between them. Assumptions:


Assumption Details


**Spec:** 1 vCPU + 2 GiB on both platforms. Blaxel's[active rate](https://blaxel.ai/pricing) of $0.0000115 per GB of RAM per second works out to the same $0.083 per hour at 2 GB.


**Session spacing:** each gap exceeds Daytona's idle window, so every session trips the full auto-stop period.


**Tuned Daytona:** we assume Daytona accepts a 1-minute auto-stop value.


**Blaxel standby:** we assume standby after 15 seconds of inactivity; standby snapshot storage costs $0.20 per GB-month.


Results:


Platform and setting Result


**Daytona, default 15-minute auto-stop:** 25 active minutes plus 75 idle minutes bill as 100 minutes, about **$0.138** .


**Daytona, auto-stop set to 1 minute:** 25 active minutes plus five 1-minute tails, about **$0.041** .


**Blaxel:** 25 active minutes plus five 15-second tails, about **$0.037** including standby snapshot storage.


[Blaxel comes in 73% cheaper than Daytona](https://blaxel.ai/blog/blaxel-vs-daytona.html) at the default. Once you tune auto-stop to a minute, the gap narrows to about 11% on unrounded figures. But a 1-minute window also stops the sandbox during slow LLM calls, so chatty agents restart more. For agents that make frequent[tool calls](https://blaxel.ai/blog/what-is-llm-function-calling) with little idle time, all three platforms cost about the same.

## 5 Daytona alternatives for AI agent sandboxes


The list starts with the three Firecracker microVM platforms (Blaxel, E2B, Vercel Sandbox). Cloudflare's Containers-based sandboxes and GPU-first Modal follow, each in the same template.


### 1. Blaxel: perpetual standby on Firecracker microVMs


[Blaxel](https://blaxel.ai/) is the infrastructure foundation for autonomous agents that execute code in production, and its Sandboxes provide that[execution environment](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-agent-runtime-environment) . Each[sandbox environment](https://blaxel.ai/blog/what-is-a-sandbox-environment) is a Firecracker microVM that drops into[standby when connections close](https://blaxel.ai/blog/understand-the-lifecycle-of-a-blaxel-sandbox) . It resumes in under 25ms with filesystem, memory, and running processes intact.


**Best for:** coding agents and PR review agents that idle between bursts of execution and need the next run to feel instant.


**Pros:**


- **Unlimited standby:** Standby bills storage only, with no time limit.
- **Exact-state resume:** Resume restores the exact prior state, so a PR review agent picks up a cloned repo without cloning again.
- **Compliance and storage:** SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HIPAA through a Business Associate Agreement (BAA);[Volumes](https://docs.blaxel.ai/Volumes/Overview) add guaranteed long-term persistence beyond standby snapshots.


**Cons:**


- **Fewer SDKs:** SDKs cover Python, TypeScript, and Go; Daytona adds Ruby and Java.
- **No GPUs:** CPU-only, so GPU workloads belong on Daytona or Modal.
- **No air-gapped option:** Blaxel covers on-premise needs through bring-your-own-metal and private networking.


**Pricing**


- **Free:** Up to $200 in free credits plus usage costs
- **Pre-configured sandbox tiers and usage-based pricing:** See[Blaxel's pricing page](https://blaxel.ai/pricing) for the most up-to-date pricing information
- **Available add-ons:** Email support, live Slack support, HIPAA compliance


### 2. E2B: open-source microVMs with plan-gated limits


E2B runs each sandbox in a Firecracker microVM and keeps an open-source repository with integration examples. Its documentation quotes about 80ms to load a saved sandbox, while a separate tutorial reports sub-200ms cold starts; its compute rates match Daytona's.


**Best for:** teams validating agent concepts who want microVM isolation and active integration examples before committing to a plan.


**Pros:**


- **SOC 2 and retention:** SOC 2 Type II per[E2B's security docs](https://docs.e2b.dev/faq/security-and-compliance) , with paused sandboxes retained without a time limit.
- **Network controls:** Egress allow and deny lists, with[secrets injection](https://docs.e2b.dev/secrets) in private beta.


**Cons:**


- **Plan-gated limits:** The plan fee gates session length and concurrency. Hobby stops at 1 hour and 20 concurrent sandboxes; Pro allows 24 hours and 100 concurrent sandboxes.
- **Enterprise minimum:** Enterprise carries a[$3,000 per month minimum](https://pricing.e2b.dev/) .


**Pricing:** Hobby is free with a[$100 one-time credit](https://e2b.dev/pricing) and no card; Pro is $150 per month plus usage.


### 3. Vercel Sandbox: active-CPU billing for I/O-bound agents


[Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/sandbox) runs Firecracker microVMs and auto-snapshots on stop. Billing counts active CPU rather than wall-clock time, which favors agents that mostly wait on an LLM.


**Best for:** TypeScript teams already on Vercel whose agents are I/O-bound and finish inside a day.


**Pros:**


- **Active-CPU billing:**[Vercel's own example](https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox) prices a 1 vCPU, 2 GB sandbox at 10% CPU for an hour at $0.0552. Full wall-clock billing would be $0.1704.
- **Pro limits:** Pro raises the ceiling to 24-hour sessions and 10,000 concurrent sandboxes.


**Cons:**


- **Session caps:** Sessions cap at 45 minutes on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro, so long-running work must stop and resume from a snapshot.
- **Short default timeout:** Sandboxes stop after 5 minutes by default, so longer agent sessions need an explicit timeout setting.


**Pricing:** Hobby is free with 5 hours of active CPU per month; Pro is $20 per user per month with $20 in monthly usage credit. Our[Vercel Sandbox alternatives](https://blaxel.ai/blog/vercel-sandbox-alternatives) guide covers the tiers in more depth.


### 4. Cloudflare Sandboxes: edge execution with ephemeral state


Cloudflare Sandboxes gives[Workers applications](https://workers.cloudflare.com/) a full Linux environment on the Containers platform, billed in 10 ms increments. Cloudflare's overview now describes each instance as a microVM, following an[architecture change](https://blog.cloudflare.com/faster-agent-sandboxes) .


**Best for:** teams already on Workers whose agents finish inside one session and need nothing from it afterward.


**Pros:**


- **State outside the sandbox:** Workers Key-Value (KV) and Durable Objects are available on the same account for state you keep after the session.
- **Workers-native:** Teams already on Workers add code execution on the same Cloudflare account, without a second vendor.


**Cons:**


- **Ephemeral by default:** State is lost after the sandbox sleeps unless written to Durable Objects or KV.
- **Three rate cards:** Costs span Containers, Workers, and Durable Objects, so a per-agent bill takes three rate cards to predict.


**Pricing:** A paid Workers plan plus usage on the three rate cards above.


### 5. Modal: GPU-first sandboxes for Python teams


[Modal](https://modal.com/) is a Python-first serverless platform with GPUs from T4 to B200. Its gVisor-isolated sandboxes default to a 5-minute lifetime. gVisor is a step up from plain containers, but microVMs add a hardware-enforced boundary.


**Best for:** machine learning teams whose agents need GPU inference next to code execution, or who already run functions on Modal.


**Pros:**


- **One account for GPU and CPU:** An agent can execute code and call a GPU model without a second vendor.
- **No idle fees:** Sandboxes bill only while they run.


**Cons:**


- **Price multipliers:** Sandboxes use the[non-preemptible tier at 3x](https://modal.com/docs/guide/preemption) the base function rate.[Regional multipliers](https://modal.com/docs/guide/region-selection) start at 1.15x for US regions.
- **Lifetime cap:** Sandboxes stop at 24 hours; longer work resumes from a filesystem snapshot.


**Pricing:** Starter is free with $30 in monthly credits and Team is $250 per month on[Modal's pricing page](https://modal.com/pricing) . The table rate applies before multipliers. See[our Modal pricing guide](https://blaxel.ai/blog/modal-pricing-alternatives-guide) for the multiplier math.


## How to choose the right Daytona alternative


Match the platform to how your agents spend idle time and what code they execute:


- **Choose Daytona** if you need H100 sandboxes, Ruby or Java SDKs, or startup credits for short, bursty jobs.
- **Choose Blaxel** if your coding or PR review agents idle between runs and need to resume with state intact under hardware isolation.
- **Choose E2B** if you want open-source microVMs and your sessions fit inside Pro's 24-hour cap.
- **Choose Cloudflare Sandboxes** if you build on Workers and your workloads can start from an empty workspace; sessions within a sandbox share its filesystem.
- **Choose Modal** if GPU inference and code execution must share one bill.


Next step: pick two finalists and run the five-session test from the pricing section against both, measuring billed minutes and resume latency on your own agent.


## Run the numbers on your own workload


Test idle cost and resume time on your own traffic before signing, because both depend on how your agents pause. Default settings that look trivial on one sandbox multiply across thousands of sandboxes a day. Agent infrastructure platforms like Blaxel keep sandboxes in standby indefinitely at zero compute charge and resume them with state intact. Blaxel builds[sandbox templates from Dockerfiles](https://docs.blaxel.ai/Sandboxes/Templates) , so Dockerfiles used for Daytona images can be adapted to build Blaxel templates by including Blaxel’s required` sandbox-api` binary. See[Blaxel Sandboxes](https://blaxel.ai/platform/sandboxes) for platform details, and compare its standby workflow with E2B's paused sandboxes or Vercel Sandbox's snapshots. Blaxel's evaluation options include[Book a demo](https://blaxel.ai/contact) for a workload walkthrough with its engineers and[sign up for free](https://app.blaxel.ai/) for testing on starter credits. Use the same workload to evaluate your other finalist.


## FAQs about Daytona dev environment pricing


### How much does Daytona cost?


Daytona bills each Daytona sandbox per second with no minimum, at the rates in the pricing section above. A 1 vCPU, 2 GiB sandbox costs about 8 cents an hour. Starter and startup credits don't cover GPU sandboxes, and idle minutes before auto-stop bill at the active rate.


### Does Daytona use containers or microVMs?


Both, depending on class. The default container class gives each sandbox dedicated namespaces and resource limits. Linux VM and Windows classes run a full virtual machine with its own kernel. For code an LLM wrote, microVM isolation is the safer default. A kernel exploit inside a container can reach the host kernel and neighboring tenants. Daytona's VM classes provide that boundary.


### What happens when a Daytona sandbox goes idle?


Container and GPU sandboxes auto-stop after 15 minutes of inactivity by default. Linux VM and Windows classes pause after 60 minutes. Stopped and paused sandboxes bill for disk only; GPU and ephemeral sandboxes are deleted on stop. Set the auto-stop interval to 0 to run indefinitely, or set a time-to-live (TTL) to delete sandboxes on a schedule.


### Which Daytona alternative fits coding agents?


Coding agents pause constantly: the user reads output, the model thinks, a test suite runs. Blaxel suits that pattern because the sandbox parks at zero compute cost between steps. It resumes with the repo, dependencies, and running dev server intact. E2B fits if sessions finish within a day, and Vercel Sandbox fits TypeScript teams on Vercel. Our guide to[code execution sandboxes](https://blaxel.ai/blog/code-execution-sandboxes-for-ai-agents) for AI agents walks through the comparison in more depth.
